extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (novelists and short-story writers) deciding which point of view to use
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for fiction writers on selecting between first-person and third-person point of view (or a hybrid), weighing voice, genre conventions, narrative needs (immediacy vs. outside knowledge), market trends, and practical tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person is the safer/publisher-friendly default
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, the third-person point of view is more common in publishing and is usually accepted by all publishers and agents without complaint; bestselling titles are majority third-person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests the 'first choice' would seemingly be third-person because editors rarely ask authors to change a novel from third-person to first-person (the reverse is more likely). Consider that market norms may reflect reasons you should examine for your own novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor your natural writing voice
rubrics_metrics.description: If you naturally tend to write one way, stick with that. Trust your 'creative' gut; if first-person comes naturally and flows, that's your voice and you should honor it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversely, if one POV is anathema to you or unsustainable, avoid it even if it's more popular. Writing that flows for you will likely be stronger and more sustainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider what you most enjoy reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about which point of view you most enjoy as a reader; if you like reading it, writing it will probably come more intuitively to you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading preferences can be a reliable indicator of the POV that suits your sensibilities and strengths as a writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-specific requirements may mandate first-person
rubrics_metrics.description: Some genres require a first-person POV, or they won't work at all (e.g., epistolary fiction, autobiographical-style fiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases like epistolary or autobiographical fiction, third-person is not really an option; choose first-person for those forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person creates immediacy and subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person is great for generating immediacy and easily brings the reader into the subjective experience of the narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first-person when you want the reader fully immersed in the protagonist's interior life and subjective perception. It's effective for intimacy and voice-driven narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person enables out-of-character perspective and omniscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-person, while less immediately intimate, allows the writer to convey things about the character and events that the character may not know; it can be omniscient or at least more knowledgeable than the character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-person gives license to leave clues or foreshadowing that the character misses, enabling broader narrative control and signaling of future events to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use third-person for mysteries requiring external foreshadowing
rubrics_metrics.description: If you need to drop clues for the reader about what’s happening that the character may not perceive, third-person is better because it can present foreshadowing outside the character’s perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For mystery novels where the reader must see information beyond the protagonist’s awareness, third-person accommodates that without breaking narrative logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first-person to conceal information (unreliable/limited narrator)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you intend to hide facts from the reader for suspense, first-person can serve your purpose because the character’s limited perspective helps obscure things until you choose to reveal them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-person is useful for unreliable narrators or plots that depend on the protagonist's ignorance; it naturally restricts what the reader knows to what the narrator perceives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid/separated narrator-protagonist approaches can combine strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: You can separate your narrator and protagonist—have the protagonist acted in third-person while a disembodied first-person narrator injects commentary or knows more than the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'in-between' space can add depth, irony, or humor, but it is uncommon and must be done well. Examples like Virginia Woolf’s Orlando show how a biographer-style narrator can provide details beyond the protagonist's knowledge. Avoid being heavy-handed if the narrator becomes the author's mouthpiece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of heavy-handed authorial commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: If the narrator functions as the author's mouthpiece, don't be too heavy-handed with that voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep authorial commentary measured; too much direct authorial intrusion can undermine narrative subtlety or frustrate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check marketplace/genre trends before deciding
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the most prevalent trend in your genre; scan bestsellers (e.g., via Amazon previews) to see whether first- or third-person dominates and reflect on why that choice might work for those books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If many successful writers make the same choice there may be reasons relevant to your novel; if not, you can still go your own way, especially if your gut argues otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small-scale experiments and reader feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: If undecided, try writing two or three short scenes from your novel in both first-person and third-person and compare which reads better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share these scenes with trusted readers (family, friends, writing group) and tally preferences as a pragmatic, 'democratic' decision method. This helps test sustainability and voice in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical sustainability of POV across a manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether you can sustain a given POV long-term; if you find you simply can’t sustain writing in one perspective, avoid it even if it’s more popular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustainability affects draft completion and overall quality; choose the POV you can maintain through a full-length work unless there are compelling narrative reasons otherwise.
